items.text: THE RITHM PROJECT YOUTH LEADERS ASK,

WHAT HAPPENS WHEN YOU BRING TOGETHER 19 PEOPLE WHO THINK ABOUT AI ALL THE TIME AND ALSO HAPPEN TO BE YOUNG TO TALK ABOUT HOW THEY’RE THINKING ABOUT AI IN THEIR LIVES RIGHT NOW AND FOR THE WORLD AT LARGE?
click through for an exploration of co-creation -->

Back at the first summit in 2023, a previously disconnected group of people came together, curious what a summit on “Human Connection + AI” would look like. It was exploratory for both the organizers and the attendees, a practice in co-creation. The Rithm Project emerged as a reaction to a shared feeling among educators, policymakers, technologists, students and parents (the point is that it was everyone) that AI was already impacting our relationships, governance, judicial system and election integrity. We had hopes for emerging technology to contribute to beneficial change, but we were seeing anything but. Maybe the technology was moving faster than we, as consumers, could benefit from it. There are so many chatbots, but where are our cures for cancer, or water filtration systems, or grid optimizations, or global food supply optimization? These may seem like big questions for a kid to ask, but we tell children to go into the workforce to do good by curing cancer and making the world a better place. So why isn’t technology doing that when added to the workforce?
items.title: THE RITHM REVIEW

items.text:
These were the questions that brought the youth leaders at this retreat into conversations about AI. What did it mean, not just for our own minds, but for the world and our future? As a generation that grew up on the internet¹ and were early users of social media, experiencing many of its negative cognitive and social effects, we see a parallel between the rise of AI and the rise of the like button or the comment section. What happens when people can say whatever they want to a digital interface? And now, what happens when they can say whatever they want and ALSO get a response?

Technology is part of who we are, whether we’re Gen Z, Gen Alpha, or millennials. It shaped the earliest parts of our lives, when learning is fastest, and some things are going wrong. There are signs that leaning on AI means less critical thinking². Students are using AI for schoolwork³ and can cheat on exams more easily than ever, though not more often than before⁴. But AI has also given us great educational resources⁵ and has made accessibility a core value of a lot of AI companies; whether that’s a form of greenwashing⁶, we won’t get into here. So we brought together 19 people between 18 and 25 to talk about what it’s like to think about AI critically while also having it integrated easily into our lives, because we are digital natives.

At the first-ever Rithm Youth Retreat, we welcomed the new Rithm Youth Fellows into the cohort, alongside youth leaders already familiar with the Rithm community, to see what would happen when The Rithm Project held a summit with young people dominating the room. Here’s what we talked about, steps for action, and the resources we’d like to offer as our work. It draws on notes, transcripts, recordings, physical media, art, and inference and analysis by the Rithm youth leaders. We’ll provide citations where necessary, but this is mostly about how youth leaders are feeling about the mental and physical space AI takes up in their lives. Our digital upbringings are the reason we are scared, so this is a practice in honesty about our fears, given the hindsight of growing up with technology.

items.text:
Hi I’m Rhea, one of the attendees! This lil digimag was created by me and thus is just one of the 19+ perspectives that created this project. That being said, I hope you take what you find in here as my experience and distillation of the retreat, both as comprehensive, but with an angle. This work is surely biased by my own interests and background and is commentary in some places. If some text was prompted for by me from AI it is underlined as AI/synthetic. If not, it is either a quote or my own writing that could be spellchecked by AI. The primary chatbot I used was Claude and I also used Claude CoWork in building myself a zine editing tool for my specific purposes (which I plan to make open source!). Anyways, yeah feel free to disagree, this little experiment’s purpose is to generate dialogue with the discussion we had together over a few days as a starting point.

Rereading is a practice I’ve rediscovered in my college years, partially because university makes you reread texts and interpret them in one million ways and in novel ones, although this practice has been done thousands of times, somehow we always have something novel to say. We have optimized ai to be pretty consistent in its outputs thus far. Let’s not unlearn what it means to interpret what already exists in order to create something new. Let’s remember what novelty means to us, what it meant to us as a kid, the feelings that arise and how those feelings may be used and moved around by the world in ways you don’t understand. I hope that the youth leaders reading this feel like they have, in a sense, re read the retreat through this review, and thus, learn to interpret what we created in new ways. This review is just one way. Explore other parts of this website for more!

items.title: Connection Committee

items.text: An overwhelming feeling in the room was that when we talked about AI, all of us felt like we were leading blind, being pro- and anti-AI at the same time. Do you need to take a binary stance on AI to lead others in understanding? Is it possible to effectively lead in the gray? What is the importance of the gray? The term “black box” was popularized by W. Ross Ashby’s An Introduction to Cybernetics (1956): a device you can only study through its inputs and outputs. Behaviorism treated the mind the same way, as something psychology could only study from the outside, and that idea fell out of favor in the cognitive revolution, when people came to think that what happens inside the mind could give us answers: about human connection, how we connect with other people, and how we think about our problems and the people in our lives. Human data is embedded in the systems we use to understand computational systems as well. Just trying to make sense of all of it: does it even matter? Is it productive for research? Is it productive in all parts of our lives? What should AI be used for, if it is the technology of the future that will probably make a lot of people’s lives better? Who are the voices we don’t talk about? What are the communities that don’t have the privilege to care about this issue as much as we do, and how might the decisions we make at scale affect them in unintended ways? The funny thing is that all the ugly mess is the part that needs to be abstracted upon to create things like computational theory, and the same abstraction is what creates our metrics of clean or messy, or even simple words like “good” or “bad.”

Built from what we told them beforehand: our hopes, what we were holding, what was adding friction.

• Introductions: name and pronouns, then doodle “the village that raised you” around ages 9 to 12.
• Family roles (slide): What role did you fill in your family? What role gave you a sense of belonging? What role did you learn to play; what was praised?
• Roles slide: Old Soul, Responsible One, Protector, Peacemaker, Mediator, Confidant, Provider, Strong One, Independent One, Invisible One, Easy Child, Sensitive One, Worrier, Baby, Rebel, Truth-Teller, Free Spirit.
• Glenda and Chris shared their own stories.
• The child enters the room with the leader: picture the old role in your leadership now. What might it be protecting? Honor what it helped you do. What does it cost you now? What might you practice instead?
• The 11 C’s: stand by a C you’re already strong in, talk about it, then move to one you want to practice more.
• Eight healing pathways: walk to the one you want more of.
• From understanding into embodiment: chairs aside, lie down, blindfolds, a three-part breath with music, then journaling.

Much of our discussion from here on will involve a map of sticky notes across the 8 domains that Rithm identified. Kash and Hannah led us in an ecosystem mapping, an exercise they brought to talk about the eight domains project. This issue with human connection and AI, if you can call that an issue, is more like a value. But what I also sensed from the room, as the narrator here, is that the value of the Rithm Project to us was that it tied us to the value of wanting to preserve some things, even though we’re really OK with change. We are a generation that is OK with change and wants to enact it as well. We’re not necessarily protesting to be conservative, but instead to embrace a future where we have the things that we still admire about today. OK, this missed a lot of my message, but we ended off by saying we’re not necessarily progressive or conservative, but instead want to embrace a future where we have what we still admire about today. There’s beauty in that admiration, and there’s also real want and fear and hope, and also happiness. I think it’s the love we have for what we do that makes us unwilling to retire. It’s not people acting out of fear or guilt. It’s about people who feel so grateful for the lives that they’ve been given so far.

items.text: [To come: for each domain, the problem that was there before AI, how AI changed it, and the feeling that it’s out of our control, told through the October sticky notes and transcript lines]
Also in November: “Connection Grift” warns that gurus, tech companies and big nonprofits could capture this moment of civic renewal and the craze for connection.
What words we used
Made by code Claude wrote: it counted how many sticky notes each word appears on, after dropping filler words like “the” and “and”. 165 notes; the 5 hidden notes are left out.
“ai” is on 40 notes, “people” on 23, “connection” on 20. [Rhea’s reading of this to come]
The gap

And still, we see we have a lot of fear, and between it and all of the projects we’re working on, which are for the hopes we have, there’s a huge gap. None of these projects primarily address our fears. Maybe this means safety work is really important, or more projects like the Rithm Project that try to instill values in the people who read its content, and explain why having a community, or just a place to express a single basic value you share, matters. For some people that’s religion; for some people that’s ethnicity, culture or hometown. But for the youth leaders at the summit, the comforts we have in the spaces that make us feel protected and seen are separate from the problem: technology isn’t in our hands. It’s often forced on us nowadays (see the lawsuits about AI in schools), and we don’t have a clear way to turn off Google’s AI Overviews. At work, jobs used to be an application of schooling; now it’s prompting instead of applying skills, teaching skills instead of using them. That is a real fear: losing jobs, fearfully holding on to a job. It is so paralyzing.

items.title: Rhea writes
items.text: Workshops were about wanting system change and thinking about how to do that while tapping into our local communities. What can we do in our daily lives, as a practice, to make system change feel easier? Is it less data center use on your personal laptop? Is it telling human stories effectively? Is it about facilitation and mediation in your digital and physical communities? For students that are searching for answers, in a field with so few, what can we provide them with? How can we distill what we know into a network of knowledge from experience rather than the knowledge of a large language model? How do we make ourselves MORE helpful than a chatbot, given our diverse yet curated (believing that human connection is at risk) perspectives on ai?
Further reading, a counterpoint: “Using ChatGPT is not bad for the environment” (Andy Masley) ↗

items.title: Closing notes
items.text:
At the start of this review I talked about how many of us were brought to this work bc of our connection to technology or technology’s relationship to our communities but I want to end this review by reminding the reader that we didn’t understand that relationship until we had it. We had no part in creating that relationship and only pursue these questions because we enjoy pursuing them. The pursuit is of fulfillment because it is filled with love and art and laughter and grace and gratitude. It’s hard to control the world around us but you can always control your response (thank you, therapist). Every single Rithm Youth Leader I’ve met cares about their agency, partially because it’s never been so at risk, but realizing how little control over our agency we may have, you can learn to react in ways that are fulfilling. To my friends that are scared of doing what they love because of what that might mean for their position in the workforce in the future, priorities in the future may change too, and although super unpractical, deeply think about what you love RIGHT NOW. I’m hesitant to say “While you can” because I’m optimistic we will figure this out with a lot of hard work, but I do hope you feel a sense of urgency to throw yourselves into the work that feels like leisure today. Your involvement and passion could preserve your passions as a lucrative endeavor for just a little bit longer. Tell your friends to perform and sing and play games. Ask for favors from your community and give back. Recognize the relational infrastructures around you and remember that you can learn from the people that built them. To end my review, and to encapsulate what this review process was like, I’ll say that we people are so good at creating. It’s practically all we do. I mean the first toothpick had to have been made out of some baby’s teething toy. We create and then we take stock and then we use and create. I think more and more we forget to take stock. Reading back my journals and notes and collecting the thoughts and art of my peers made me understand our words as JUST MOMENTS of a 72 hour trip. Collecting is also something we people are great at, and something I’m terrible at (hoarding). Although the Library of Alexandria and preservation of physical material has led to losses of knowledge throughout history, sometimes, that loss is the only way we have enough space to create something new. I remember taking a trip to Alpine Meadows and walking in a forest that had burned down around a decade ago. I remember feeling extremely sad as a young middle schooler, thinking about the surrounding forested mountains and this desolate patch of burned still ash ridden land. The naturalist explaining the scene was undisturbed. I shared that lack of disturbance when I visited again as a high schooler, a couple years later, and had noticed that the straw colored ground was just a little bit more green.

I believe in ebbs and flows and tides and turns and I think through all of it, we have to make sure to take stock of where we are and what we have. As a lover of the natural sciences I often think about the law of conservation and the idea that entropy is ever increasing in the universe. I can’t really wrap my head around it for no particular reason. It makes me think that we are somehow never-ending but always redistributing, renegotiating with all the space in the universe, somewhere there’s an equilibrium, and one day that equilibrium will be perturbed and 100 years after that it will still be settling into its homeostasis or rhythm. And that redistribution, is how I see path forward in this confusing and complex new time in a young person’s lives. Never in our lives have people our age consumed more than we do in the 21st century. 2000’s kids grew up with the internet, increasing the content and overall amount of information we consumed by the time we were 5. We aren’t sure how our brains work but instead of waiting for neuroscience and biological research to catch up, we can help out by understanding ourselves. Understanding how what we’ve consumed and the experiences we’ve had connect. We’re doing a good job of this right now [citation and also social media cases], and we should keep it up. Like I say at the beginning of a game of concentration. [Concentration, concentration is a game. Keep the rithm, keep the rithm or ur lame.]
Pew Research Center (2025): 48% of teens say social media is mostly bad for people their age, and 44% have cut back ↗
The first social media addiction trial (Los Angeles, March 2026): a jury found Meta and YouTube negligent ↗

items.title: People
items.text: About 20 young people (ours were 18 to 25), some new to each other and some returning. Two organizers who were also participants: Kash and Hannah, Rithm fellows. Guests to lead one workshop: Glenda and Chris. Home groups of three or four who checked in at the start and end of each day.

items.title: Teams
items.text:
Most people joined a committee, picked from a preference form:
• Story & Momentum: photos, notes, the zine table
• Food Crew: planned and cooked the group meals
• Connection: welcomes, recovery time, the grounding activity

items.title: Delegation
items.text: Every block on the plan had an owner, and most were not the organizers: travel and the mapping (Hannah), the welcome and energizers (Odist), letters and the card game (Kash), breakouts (workshop leaders), meals (Food Crew), the network walk (Story & Momentum). Each break had a poem, read by a different person.

items.title: Questions
items.text:
The plan gave each part of the day one question:
• “Can we see the big picture”
• “What do we WANT the future to be?”
• “How will we get there”
• “What needs to be true about my own career and skills so that I can play a role in how we get there?”
And to close: “One thing learned, one thing changed, one thing to carry forward.”

items.title: Games
items.text: The AI Effect card game (support, erode, or it depends). Odist’s chair game. A blanket-drop name game. A confession jar: “anonymously drop in one way you’ve used AI you wouldn’t normally admit.” After hours: mafia, Secret Hitler, Codenames, karaoke, cards.

items.title: Food
items.text: Three meals cooked together: a build-your-own dinner on Friday, dinner on Saturday, breakfast on Sunday. Snacks, water and drinks set out for arrival. Sandwiches for the trip home made at Sunday breakfast. The Food Crew left the session before dinner early to start cooking.

items.title: Supplies + materials
items.text: Sticky notes and a sheet of paper on the floor for each of the eight domains. A printed workbook for each person. Envelopes and cards for the letters, and blank postcards. A zine table with art supplies, watercolors and old Rithm materials. A Polaroid camera. Mats and blindfolds for the breathwork. A TV for slides, and a shared playlist.

items.title: What we did with it
items.text:
The shape of our weekend
Friday, “Arrive + Land”: welcome, home groups, dinner, a letter to next year’s you, game night.
Saturday, “Explore + Expand”: a morning workshop on leadership identity, the card game, ecosystem mapping in the afternoon, then three rounds of 30-minute workshops led by participants, and a mutual aid session.
Sunday, “Connect + Carry Forward”: a network walk through the map, an action lab, closing reflection, a grounding activity.

Consultancy workshops
Practical Skills & Career Building
· Bomi: “Identity and your locus of control: naming and overcoming the fears that may stall your professional development”
· Leorah: “A debate workshop focused not on winning, but on productive conversation - making sure both sides feel heard across divides”
AI, Futures & Society
· Leo: “What might an ‘AGI’ future look like and how might we prepare?”
· Audrey: “Making sense of AI news right now, plus feedback on a program bridging AI safety x AI impacts on humans/ society.”
· Marisol: personal AI project feedback (her talk: “Is Small AI a Suitable Alternative?”)
· Dylan: “Storytelling workshop - how narrative shapes us and helps us find connectivity through the stories we tell about ourselves”

José: a poem, “You, If No One Else”
Playlist + credits
Scan for our playlist. The full team page is on the site.
